name: journal-made-of-a-woman.json
content:
What does Paul say about the birth of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him)? One clause. Galatians says God sent his Son, "born of woman, born under the law".1 The woman has no name. There is no angel, no Bethlehem, no shepherd and no virgin. Everything the church later tells about the birth comes from other books.

That makes the clause worth reading slowly, because it is the whole of Paul's evidence.

What the clause says

Paul is arguing with the Galatians about the Torah. His point is that God sent the Son at the right moment to "redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons".2 The birth is there as a premise. The Son came as a human being, from a woman, and under the same law as everyone else in Israel.

[paulus_figure name="photo-newborn-hand"]A newborn's hand. Paul gives the birth of ʿĪsā one clause: "born of woman" (Galatians 4:4).[/paulus_figure]

Two other places add a line each. In Romans the Son "was descended from David according to the flesh",3 and in Philippians he took the form of a servant, "being born in the likeness of men".4 Between them these three verses are all of it. Paul names no mother and no town. He gives no date and tells no story of the child.

What is missing

The Gospel of Matthew quotes Isaiah on the virgin who will conceive and bear a son.5 Paul never cites that verse. He never mentions Mary, Joseph or Nazareth. He does not tell the Corinthians, who were arguing about everything else, that the child had no human father.

Paul says nothing either way. A man who thought the miraculous conception was the proof of his Lord's divinity would have used it. Paul reaches for the resurrection every time. In Romans the Son is "declared to be the Son of God in power" by the resurrection,6 and the declaration comes at the end of his life on earth, not at the start of it. [paulus_link slug="what-paul-never-said-about-jesus" /] lists more of what the letters leave out.

Born under the law

The second half of the clause deserves as much weight as the first. ʿĪsā was born under the law. He lived as a Jew, kept the Torah and taught in the synagogues of Galilee. Paul says so in the same breath in which he tells the Galatians that the law no longer binds them.

The two sit badly together. If the Son himself lived under the law, the Gentiles had no need of a different gospel. [paulus_link slug="jesus-in-his-own-words" /] collects what ʿĪsā said about the law, and none of it sounds like Galatians.

[paulus_figure name="ancient-papyrus-fragment-36505438"]A papyrus fragment. The letters of Paul, written before the Gospels, give the birth of ʿĪsā a single clause.[/paulus_figure]

A Muslim reading

The Qurʾān names the mother and gives the child a voice. In Sūrah Maryam the infant speaks from the cradle: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allāh. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet."7 His first words in that sūrah are a statement of servanthood. Paul's letters, written decades earlier, have nothing to set beside it.

Matthew, Luke and the Qurʾān agree that the mother was Maryam. The man who wrote the earliest Christian documents we have did not trouble to say so.

The verdict

Paul gives the birth of ʿĪsā three verses and no story. He never names the mother and never mentions the virgin birth that the church treats as a sign of divinity. His Christ has no mother's name and no childhood, only the word "woman".

He ties the Son's birth to the law only to tell his readers that the law is finished. A reader who goes to Paul to learn who ʿĪsā was finds a man born of a woman under the law, and then finds Paul explaining why that man's own religion no longer binds anyone. [paulus_link slug="paul-the-father-of-a-new-religion" /] follows how the letters were made to carry the divine Son of the later creeds, and [paulus_link slug="seven-doctrines" /] sets out the doctrines built on them.

Born of a woman: questions readers ask

What does Galatians 4:4 mean?

It says that God's Son was born of a woman and lived under the Mosaic law. Paul uses it to show that the Son shared the human condition of those he came to redeem.

Does Paul mention the virgin birth?

No. The letters never mention a virgin, Mary or Joseph. Matthew and Luke tell the story, and both were written after Paul's letters.

Did Paul know the Gospels?

The four Gospels in our New Testament were written after his letters. Paul quotes the Lord a handful of times and gives no sign that he had a written Gospel in front of him.

What does the Qurʾān say about the birth of ʿĪsā?

It names his mother Maryam and records that he spoke as an infant, calling himself the servant of Allāh and a prophet (Sūrah Maryam 19:30).
